newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War panic in Zaire capital, governor asks for calm.
newsitem.headline: War panic in Zaire capital, governor asks for calm.

text.p: Fear gripped the Zaire capital on Sunday as rebels said they were resuming their offensive in a final push to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Residents of the city of over five million people scrambled to stock up, sending prices soaring in city markets and a handful of shops that opened before a potentially violent anti-Mobutu protest shutdown of the city planned for Monday.
In the eastern rebel headquarter city of Goma, the rebels said they were resuming their offensive after a three-day pause to allow Mombutu to step down honourably.
Kinshasa's military governor intervened on the lunchtime national television news to urge Zaireans and foreigners to remain calm.

"An atmosphere of panic, due essentially to the situation in the east of our country, reigns among Kinshasa's men and women," General Amela Lokima said. "The most fantastic rumours according to which the city of Kinshasa would soon fall to the armed rebellion are gaining ground."
He said the army was ready to defend Kinshasa, adding, "The security of our capital is our fundamental duty".

The television announcer said panic had swept districts of Kinshasa near the airport after local anti-Mobutu militants urged residents to leave. The airport is in the direction of Bandundu Province to the northeast where rebels say they have infiltrated.
The fear of war and a looming confrontation between anti-Mobutu activists and security forces on Monday sent Kinshasa residents scrambling to snap up supplies.
"People have been stocking up since yesterday," said Mauritanian storeowner Sidi Mohamed.

His compatriot Mohamed Umar next door said shops were running out of imports: "Suppliers are not bringing in goods. We too are not buying because you don't know if your shop will be looted the next day."
He said prices of imported food had shot up in the few days since Kabila's forces seized the copper capital Lubumbashi and set their sights on Kinshasa.
"A kilo of onions from Belgium has gone up to 280,000 zaire from 240,000 zaire, " he said. The zaire was exchanging at about 180,000 to the dollar on Sunday.
Nearby, anti-Mobutu activists distributed leaflets calling for a "dead city" strike on Monday, followed by the closure of schools and colleges on Tuesday.
"It will be a total boycott, a total shutdown. No vehicle dares go on the road," declared a man called Mbambu. "We are not afraid of Mobutu or his army."

Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs commissioner in the rebel alliance, told a news conference in Goma that Kabila would probably go to South Africa soon to spur negotiations on Mobutu's departure from power.
"There will never be a ceasefire before negotiations -- never, never, never," Karaha said.
Mobutu on Saturday for the first time raised the possibility of meeting Kabila but insisted this would only be possible if Kabia asked him politely.

"If he asks me politely I cannot refuse to talk to a compatriot but (for him) to be in Goma and say I give him three days (to resign), it's not my style or nature. I cannot reply," Mobutu, 66, told reporters.

Mobutu's collapsing army has been unable to check the rebel offensive that began near Zaire's eastern border last October. Kabila's forces now hold more than half the country including most major centres outside Kinshasa.
